en: The Sutra on the Eight Awakenings of the Great Men,
spoken by the Buddha and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
As a disciple of the Buddha, one should constantly, throughout the day and night, recite and contemplate with a sincere heart these eight awakenings of the great men:
The first awakening:
The world is impermanent; lands are fragile and precarious;
the four elements are suffering and empty; the five aggregates are without self.
Arising and ceasing, changing and transforming, they are false and without a master;
the mind is the source of evil, and the physical form is a thicket of transgressions.
Observing in this way, one gradually departs from birth and death.
The second awakening:
Excessive desire is suffering; the exhaustion of birth and death arises from craving.
Few desires lead to non-action, wherein body and mind are at ease.
The third awakening:
The mind is never satisfied and seeks only to acquire more, thereby increasing evil;
the Bodhisattva is not so, for he constantly contemplates contentment, remains at peace in poverty while guarding the Way, making wisdom alone his primary task.
The fourth awakening:
realizing that indolence leads to downfall;
by constantly practicing diligence, one destroys the evils of affliction, subdues the four māras, and emerges from the prison of the aggregates and realms.
The fifth awakening is the delusion of birth and death.
The Bodhisattva constantly reflects upon this, extensively studying and hearing much, increasing wisdom, perfecting eloquence, and teaching all beings so that they may all attain great bliss.
The sixth awakening:
To be poor and suffering is to have many enemies, leading one to recklessly form evil karmic conditions.
The Bodhisattva practices giving with equal regard for both enemies and kin; he does not dwell on past wrongs nor harbor hatred toward those who do him harm.
The seventh awakening:
the faults and perils of the five desires;
though he is a layman, he is not defiled by worldly pleasures.
Constantly mindful of the three robes and the earthen bowl as the vessels of the Dharma;
aspiring to leave the household life to maintain the purity of the Way;
lofty and far-reaching in Brahma-conduct, with compassion for all beings.
The eighth awakening:
Birth and death are ablaze with fire, and suffering is immeasurable.
One gives rise to the Mahāyāna mind to universally deliver all beings.
"I vow to undergo immeasurable suffering on behalf of sentient beings,
so that all sentient beings may attain ultimate great bliss.
These eight matters are precisely what the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Great Beings have realized.
Practicing the path with vigor, cultivating wisdom through compassion, they board the ship of the Dharma-body to reach the shore of Nirvana;
yet they return once more to the realm of birth and death to deliver and liberate all sentient beings.

Using these eight matters, they guide and instruct all beings, causing sentient beings to awaken to the suffering of birth and death, to renounce the five desires, and to cultivate the holy path of the mind.
If a disciple of the Buddha recites these eight matters, in every moment of thought they shall extinguish immeasurable sins;
they shall advance toward Bodhi and swiftly ascend to perfect enlightenment;
they shall forever sever birth and death and dwell eternally in bliss.
The Sutra on the Eight Arousals of Mindfulness of the Great Men Spoken by the Buddha.
